raw_text:
Since Michel Mirowski first demonstrated the feasibility of an implantable automatic defibrillator to terminate malignant ventricular arrhythmias in 1980 [1], implantable cardioverter-defibrillators (ICDs) have revolutionized sudden cardiac death (SCD) prevention. While conventional transvenous ICDs (TV-ICDs) are highly effective, their intravascular leads present a persistent clinical vulnerability, frequently associated with long-term complications such as lead fracture, venous occlusion, and systemic endocarditis. To mitigate these vascular risks, the subcutaneous ICD (S-ICD) was developed, placing the entire system in an entirely extrathoracic position [2]. Early clinical trials quickly established the safety, efficacy, and rapid detection capabilities of this novel technology [3].

The physical configuration of the S-ICD comprises a left thoracic pulse generator and a subcutaneous parasternal lead. While S-ICDs were initially implanted using a three-incision technique, a simplified two-incision method was introduced to improve cosmetic outcomes and reduce procedure times [4]. Patient selection relies heavily on pre-implant electrocardiographic (ECG) screening, as S-ICD sensing is based on subcutaneous vectors rather than intracardiac signals. Both the manual QRS-T morphology screening tool [5] and computerized automated screening programs [6] are mandatory to ensure the device can differentiate the QRS complex from the T-wave and prevent T-wave oversensing (TWOS)—a major driver of inappropriate shocks. To improve signal quality, early software iterations utilized a discrimination algorithm to distinguish supraventricular from ventricular tachycardias [7]. Clinical registries, such as the EFFORTLESS S-ICD registry, provided vital real-world validation of S-ICD performance [8]. Concurrently, newer filtering and template matching algorithms [9] were designed to optimize sensing, leading to a steady decline in early complication rates [10]. Despite these innovations, inappropriate shocks due to cardiac and extracardiac oversensing remain a major clinical challenge [11]. When complications do arise, specialized surgical management may be required to reposition or revise S-ICD pocket sites [12]. S-ICD systems have also been increasingly applied in younger patients with inherited cardiomyopathies, such as hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) [13], and as a vital salvage therapy following the extraction of infected transvenous leads [14].

Modern implantation strategies have evolved beyond simple subcutaneous placement. The intermuscular two-incision technique—placing the generator between the serratus anterior and latissimus dorsi muscles—has shown significant improvements in patient comfort and protection against device erosion [15]. Longitudinal data from the EFFORTLESS trial reinforced the durability of the subcutaneous approach [16]. Systemic evaluations comparing the four principal implantation techniques (subcutaneous, subfascial, submuscular, and intermuscular) have helped surgeons tailor procedures to individual patient habitus [17]. Guided by current clinical guidelines [18], S-ICDs are strongly recommended for patients without pacing requirements.

To target T-wave and myopotential oversensing, the high-pass "SMART Pass" filter was developed, successfully reducing inappropriate shocks without compromising VF detection sensitivity [19]. Furthermore, the introduction of the radiographic PRAETORIAN score [20] enabled clinicians to evaluate optimal S-ICD component positioning post-implantation to predict defibrillation success. Real-world cohorts still note inappropriate shocks triggered by physiological or environmental noise [21]. However, S-ICD remains highly favorable in high-risk patients, such as those on hemodialysis, who present with compromised venous access and elevated bacteremia risk [22].

The landmark PRAETORIAN trial [23] provided the first randomized, head-to-head comparison of S-ICD and TV-ICD, demonstrating that the S-ICD is non-inferior to transvenous systems regarding the composite endpoint of inappropriate shocks and device complications. While myopotential induction during strenuous exercise can still provoke sensing failures [24], proper template setup and optimization have minimized these occurrences. Defibrillation efficacy remains excellent, with studies confirming that the standard 80-Joule S-ICD output provides a robust safety margin over lower-energy (40-Joule) defibrillation thresholds [25]. The prospective UNTOUCHED trial [26] further demonstrated that high-rate programming and contemporary sensing filters yield extremely low inappropriate shock rates in primary prevention populations with low ejection fractions, matching modern TV-ICD cohorts.

Both the American guidelines [18] and the updated European Society of Cardiology (ESC) guidelines [27] support S-ICD as a Class I/IIa recommendation for patients who do not require pacing. Long-term (5-year) results from the EFFORTLESS registry confirmed S-ICD longevity and low late-complication rates [28]. Additionally, the ATLAS randomized trial [29] demonstrated the superiority of the S-ICD over the TV-ICD in reducing serious perioperative and lead-related complications at six months.

Despite these successes, S-ICD's inability to provide anti-tachycardia pacing (ATP) or bradycardia pacing remains its primary limitation. To overcome this, the recently published MODULAR ATP trial [30] evaluated a modular cardiac rhythm management system consisting of a leadless pacemaker in wireless communication with an S-ICD. This breakthrough technology delivers co-directed ATP and pacing, signaling a new era of completely extravascular and leadless device therapies.
